content: Fat necrosis refers to a localized area of fat tissue destruction caused by the abnormal release of activated lipases. When the pancreas is injured—due to factors such as infection, toxins, viruses, trauma, or ischemia—activated pancreatic enzymes are released. These enzymes liquefy the membranes of fat cells. The lipases then break down the triglyceride esters within the fat cells, releasing fatty acids. These fatty acids combine with calcium to form visible chalky white nodules, which are characteristic of fat necrosis. Diagnostic Findings Mammogram The mammographic appearance of fat necrosis can vary widely, ranging from clearly benign to potentially malignant. Calcifications observed on mammography may present as benign ring-like or rim-like structures, coarse macrocalcifications, or, in some cases, suspicious pleomorphic or branching type microcalcifications. Ultrasound Masses associated with fat necrosis are most commonly solid but may also appear complex or cystic. The borders of these masses can be either well-defined or ill-defined. Posterior shadowing or enhancement may also be observed. MRI The signal characteristics of fat necrosis follow those of fat tissue. It appears bright on T1-weighted images, with a loss of signal on fat-saturated images. Pathological Findings: Case Study Clinical Summary A 37-year-old female with chronic renal failure underwent a renal transplant. Post-transplant, she developed a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in her nasal cavity, oral candidiasis, pneumonia, hematuria, pyuria, and gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient subsequently became septic and died. Autopsy Findings The autopsy revealed extensive hemorrhagic bronchopneumonia caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and multiple ulcers in the stomach and esophagus. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) was evident, with multiple hemorrhages present. Firm, whitish foci of necrotic tissue were identified in the fat surrounding the pancreas. Gross examination of the intestines and omentum showed small (5–15 mm) white nodules on the surface of the omental and mesenteric fat tissue. The pancreas and adjacent mesenteric fat tissue also exhibited white nodules. Microscopic Findings Low-power photomicrographs of the pancreas showed fat tissue surrounding the organ, with a rim of inflammatory cells and blue-stained areas in the fat adjacent to the pancreas. High-power photomicrographs revealed areas of inflammation and fat necrosis in the peripancreatic fat tissue. Blue discoloration in the interlobular fat spaces of the pancreas was noted, corresponding to calcium deposits within the fat cells. Granular blue-staining calcium deposits were observed within the fat cells, with clear areas representing artifacts caused by the washing out of fat during histological processing. Additional high-power images demonstrated calcifications in the interlobular spaces of the pancreas, characteristic of fat necrosis.
